note: Evergreen fallback tips for Insights of the Day v3: used only when no good fresh insight is ready, so a weekday is never skipped. Each was checked against its official docs page on 28 Nov 2026. No admin, billing or IT-approval tips. Plain hyphens only.

tips.subject: Your pandas merge might be duplicating rows
tips.preheader: One argument makes pandas shout when your join keys are not unique.
tips.context: A join on a key that is not unique quietly multiplies rows, and every total after it is wrong.
tips.tip: Add `validate="many_to_one"` (or `"one_to_one"`) to `pd.merge` so pandas raises an error when the keys are not unique.
steps: Find a `pd.merge` in your current notebook
Add `validate="many_to_one"` if the right table should have unique keys
Add `indicator=True` and check the `_merge` column for unmatched rows
tips.angle: Catch silent row blow-ups before they reach a report.

tips.subject: Find out what your DataFrame really weighs
tips.preheader: The default memory number hides your text columns. Here is the real one.
tips.context: The memory figure pandas shows by default leaves out most of what text columns cost.
tips.tip: Run `df.info(memory_usage="deep")` for the true size, then convert repeated text columns with `.astype("category")`.
steps: Pick a text column with few unique values
Convert it with `.astype("category")` and run info again
tips.angle: Smaller DataFrames and fewer out-of-memory crashes.

tips.subject: Load only the CSV columns you need
tips.preheader: Two arguments to read_csv that make big files load faster.
tips.context: Most notebooks read every column of a big CSV and then use five of them.
tips.tip: Pass `usecols=[...]` and `dtype={...}` to `pd.read_csv` so pandas skips unused columns and stops guessing types.
steps: List the columns you actually use
Add `dtype={...}` for ids and codes that should stay text
tips.angle: Faster loads, less memory, and ids that keep their leading zeros.

tips.subject: Print debugging, but with labels for free
tips.preheader: Add one character to your print and never mix up which number is which.
tips.context: A wall of bare numbers in the console is how bugs hide in plain sight.
tips.tip: Write `print(f"{total=}")` and Python prints `total=` followed by the value.
tips.angle: Readable debug output in one character.

tips.subject: Stop guessing: pause your code mid-run
tips.preheader: One built-in function beats ten print statements.
tips.context: Sprinkling print statements to find a bug takes many runs. Pausing takes one.
tips.tip: Put `breakpoint()` on the line before the bug; Python stops there and lets you inspect every variable.
steps: Run the script and type a variable name to see its value
Type `c` to continue or `q` to quit
tips.angle: Find the bug in one run instead of ten.

tips.subject: Rerun only the tests that just failed
tips.preheader: Stop waiting for the whole suite while you fix one test.
tips.context: Fixing one failing test should not mean waiting for the whole suite every time.
tips.tip: Run `pytest --lf` to rerun only the last run's failures, or `pytest --ff` to run them first and then the rest.
steps: Run `pytest --lf` until it is green, then run everything
tips.angle: Faster fix-and-check loops.

tips.subject: The back button for Git branches
tips.preheader: Toggle between two branches without typing their names.
tips.context: Typing long branch names to hop between a fix and a feature gets old fast.
tips.tip: `git switch -` takes you back to the branch you were on before, like a browser's back button.
tips.angle: Hop between branches without typing names.

tips.subject: Commit half a file, not the whole mess
tips.preheader: Stage only the lines that belong together, then commit.
tips.context: A fix and an unrelated tweak in the same file usually end up in one messy commit.
tips.tip: `git add -p` walks through each change and lets you stage only the pieces that belong in this commit.
steps: Press `y` to stage a piece, `n` to skip it
tips.angle: Clean commits that are easy to review and revert.

tips.subject: That commit you just lost is still there
tips.preheader: A bad reset or rebase is rarely the end. Here is the way back.
tips.context: After a bad reset or rebase, the work looks gone. Git usually still has it.
tips.tip: Run `git reflog` to find the commit from before the mistake and save it on a new branch.
steps: Run `git reflog` and find the line before the mistake
Run `git branch rescue <id>` to keep it safe
tips.angle: Most lost work is one command away.

tips.subject: Find what is eating your disk in Docker
tips.preheader: One command shows the space Docker uses and how much you can get back.
tips.context: Old images, stopped containers and build cache pile up until the disk is full.
tips.tip: Run `docker system df` to see how much space images, containers and volumes use, and how much is reclaimable.
steps: Free build cache with `docker builder prune`
tips.angle: Get disk space back without guessing what to delete.

tips.subject: Make your Docker builds start faster
tips.preheader: Stop sending your data folder and .git to every build.
tips.context: Every build sends the whole folder to Docker first, including data and .git.
tips.tip: Add a `.dockerignore` file so data folders, `.git` and virtual environments are left out of the build context.
steps: Rebuild and compare the context size
tips.angle: Faster builds and no secrets copied into images by accident.

tips.subject: See exactly why your SQL query is slow
tips.preheader: Two words in front of a query show where the time goes.
tips.context: Guessing which part of a slow query hurts is slow too.
tips.tip: Put `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` before a PostgreSQL query to see the real plan, row counts and time for each step.
steps: Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` followed by your SELECT
Look for a Seq Scan on a big table
For UPDATE or DELETE, wrap it in `BEGIN` and `ROLLBACK`, because it really runs
tips.angle: Fix the step that is slow instead of rewriting everything.

tips.subject: Your cross-validation score may be too good
tips.preheader: One wrapper stops test data from leaking into training.
tips.context: Scaling the whole dataset before cross-validation lets test data leak into training.
tips.tip: Put scaling and other preprocessing inside a scikit-learn `Pipeline`, so it is fitted only on the training folds.
steps: Compare the score with your old one
tips.angle: Honest scores that hold up in production.

tips.subject: Keep column names after scikit-learn transforms
tips.preheader: Stop getting bare NumPy arrays back from your pipeline.
tips.context: After a transform, you get a bare array and lose track of which column is which.
tips.tip: Call `.set_output(transform="pandas")` on a transformer or pipeline so it returns DataFrames with column names.
steps: Run `fit_transform` and look at the columns
Use the names when you inspect features
tips.angle: Readable outputs and fewer column mix-ups.

tips.subject: One argument keeps rare classes in your test set
tips.preheader: A random split can leave your rare class out of the test set.
tips.context: With rare classes, a random split can leave almost none of them in the test set.
tips.tip: Pass `stratify=y` to `train_test_split` so train and test keep the same class balance.
tips.angle: Test scores you can trust on imbalanced data.

tips.subject: Preview an S3 sync before it deletes anything
tips.preheader: See every copy and delete first, then run it for real.
tips.context: One wrong path in an S3 sync with delete can wipe the wrong folder.
tips.tip: Add `--dryrun` to `aws s3 sync` to list every copy and delete it would do, without doing it.
steps: Run it for real only when the list looks right
tips.angle: No surprise deletes in shared buckets.

tips.subject: Edit every copy of a word at once
tips.preheader: A VS Code shortcut that turns ten edits into one.
tips.context: Changing the same word in ten places by hand is slow and easy to get wrong.
tips.tip: In VS Code, select a word and press `Ctrl+D` (`Cmd+D` on Mac) to add the next match, then type once to edit them all.
steps: Press `Ctrl+D` for each next match, or `Ctrl+Shift+L` for all
tips.angle: Ten edits in one go.

tips.subject: Settle the 'which is faster' debate in one line
tips.preheader: Stop arguing about speed. Measure it in your notebook.
tips.context: Opinions about which pandas approach is faster are cheap. Measuring is cheaper.
tips.tip: In Jupyter, put `%timeit` before a line of code to time it over many runs and get a fair average.
tips.angle: Speed decisions based on numbers, not hunches.

tips.subject: Stop Claude mixing up your instructions and data
tips.preheader: A simple prompt habit from Anthropic's own guide.
tips.context: Long prompts with pasted documents blur where your instructions end and the data starts.
tips.tip: Wrap each document in tags like `<contract>` and `</contract>`, and refer to the tag name in your instructions.
steps: Write the task outside the tags
Ask for the answer inside tags like `<answer>`
tips.angle: Clearer prompts and answers that are easy to pull out.

tips.subject: Make AI answers stick to your document
tips.preheader: Three lines in your prompt cut made-up answers.
tips.context: Ask a model about a long document and it may fill gaps with confident guesses.
tips.tip: Ask Claude to pull direct quotes from the document first, answer only from those quotes, and allow it to say it does not know.
steps: Add: First quote the relevant passages
Add: Answer only from those quotes
Add: If the document does not say, say you do not know
tips.angle: Answers you can check against the source.

tips.subject: Show Gemini an example instead of explaining
tips.preheader: Google's own prompting guide recommends this for almost every prompt.
tips.context: Long instructions about format often get ignored. A good example rarely does.
tips.tip: Add 2 or 3 examples of the exact output you want to your Gemini prompt; Google's guide recommends few-shot examples.
steps: Write the task in one line
Paste 2 or 3 example inputs with ideal outputs
tips.angle: Consistent format and tone with less instruction text.

tips.subject: Split a list into chunks without index maths
tips.preheader: A Python 3.12 one-liner for APIs with batch limits.
tips.context: Chunking a list for an API with a batch limit usually means fiddly index maths.
tips.tip: `itertools.batched(items, 100)` gives you tuples of up to 100 items at a time, in order.
steps: Check you are on Python 3.12 or newer
Send each batch to the API
tips.angle: Cleaner loops and no off-by-one chunk bugs.
